name: Data rights and provenance
summary: Tracking where training data came from, what licence it carries and whether its owners opted out, and the legal questions still open.

D1.guide: Guess first: if a website says 'no robots', does the crawler have to listen?
text: Every piece of training data was made by someone. Some of it is free to use, some has rules, and some owners say no.
Provenance means keeping a record of where each piece came from, so people can check it was allowed.
D1.analogy: Checking the label on every ingredient: where it came from and whether you may use it.

text: **Provenance** is the record of a dataset's sources, licences and processing steps. Many public datasets are re-packaged from others, and licence details often get lost or mislabelled along the way.

**Opt-outs** let owners signal that they don't want their work used: a `robots.txt` rule aimed at a crawler, website terms, or machine-readable reservations. Honouring them is partly voluntary and partly a legal duty, depending on the country.

**The law is still settling.** Courts in several countries are weighing whether training on copyrighted work without permission is allowed, and some regions now require model makers to publish summaries of their training data.

diagram.caption: The questions a piece of data should pass

D2.analogy: Food labelling: every ingredient should be traceable back to the farm, with its allergens listed.
D2.analogyBreaks: Food can be recalled from shelves. Once data has shaped a model's weights there is no reliable way to take it back out, so an opt-out mostly affects future training runs.

predict.question: A website adds a rule blocking AI crawlers today. What happens to models already trained on its pages?
options: Nothing changes; the rule only affects future crawls
predict.explanation: robots.txt is read at crawl time. It cannot reach into weights that already exist, which is why removing data after training ('machine unlearning') is an open research problem.

text: Big legal questions remain open: whether training counts as fair use or falls under text and data mining exceptions, what is owed when a model reproduces training text, and how opt-outs should work at web scale.
Restricting crawlers protects owners but can shrink the open data commons, favouring organisations that already hold data or can pay for licences.

sources.title: The Data Provenance Initiative: A Large Scale Audit of Dataset Licensing & Attribution in AI
Consent in Crisis: The Rapid Decline of the AI Data Commons
